props.title: Time to Leave

sections.content: François Ozon's devastating Time to Leave marks a pivotal moment in French cinema's exploration of mortality. The film follows a gay fashion photographer facing terminal cancer, echoing the raw emotional territory of Philadelphia (1993) but with Ozon's characteristic French intimacy. Unlike melodramatic terminal illness films like Sweet November (2001), Ozon strips away sentimentality to focus on one man's complex journey of acceptance. The result shares DNA with Ikiru (1952) and The Death of Mr. Lazarescu (2005) in its unflinching look at facing death.

sections.content: Melvil Poupaud's nuanced performance as Romain captures the isolation of terminal illness with remarkable restraint. The film's power lies in quiet moments - Romain photographing strangers on the beach, final conversations with his grandmother (played brilliantly by Jeanne Moreau), the way he touches fabric and light as if memorizing the world's textures. This approach influenced later intimate portraits of mortality like The Farewell (2019) and Departures (2008).

Ozon's visual language in Time to Leave creates a masterclass in showing internal struggle through external details. The way he frames Romain through windows and mirrors recalls Krzysztof Kieślowski's Blue (1993), while the beach sequences echo the existential weight of Ingmar Bergman's Wild Strawberries (1957). The film's treatment of sexuality and illness proved groundbreaking, paving the way for works like BPM (Beats Per Minute) (2017) and Sorry Angel (2018). sections.content: Time to Leave represents a crucial shift in French cinema's portrayal of death and dying. Where earlier films like The Mother and the Whore (1973) approached mortality through philosophical dialogue, Ozon creates a visceral experience through silence and gesture. This influenced contemporary French directors like Robin Campillo and Céline Sciamma in their approach to depicting personal crisis and transformation.
